title: Best practices for measuring the performance and stability of indoor photovoltaic devices - Nature Energy
gist: A consensus statement from 60+ institutions and companies proposes standardized best practices for measuring indoor photovoltaic (iPV) performance and stability, recommending CIE LED B-3 (4,000 K) as the future reference spectrum, 200 lx as the mandatory reporting illuminance, and a tiered measurement-system classification plus four base stability tests to fix the currently non-comparable field where inconsistencies reach 60%.

insights.claim: Indoor photovoltaics lacks a widely adopted universal measurement standard equivalent to solar PV's Standard Test Conditions, and the resulting variability in light sources, illumination, equipment and procedures produces performance-comparison inconsistencies reaching 60% in relative terms.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Non-comparable results across labs and vendors slow commercialization and make published iPV efficiency claims hard to trust without standardized conditions.
insights.quote: iPV lacks an equivalent widely-adopted universal standard, and the resulting variability in light sources, illumination conditions, equipment and procedures makes fair performance comparisons difficult, with inconsistencies even reaching 60% in relative terms

insights.claim: The IEC's 2023 Technical Specification IEC TS 62607-7-2 established methodologies for measuring indoor PV efficiency but left key issues unresolved, including uncertainty over whether maximum power density or power conversion efficiency should be prioritized in reporting.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Even the existing IEC spec leaves reporting ambiguity that this consensus statement aims to close by fixing the MPD-PCE relationship.

insights.claim: The authors advocate CIE LED B-3 (4,000 K) as the future best-practice reference spectrum for indoor PV evaluation, superseding the current IEC-adopted LED B-4 (5,000 K), citing market prevalence and the CIE's adoption of the identical L41 spectrum for photometer calibration.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A single agreed reference spectrum fixes the MPD-to-PCE conversion and makes cross-lab and cross-technology iPV numbers directly comparable.
insights.quote: We therefore advocate for CIE LED B-3 (4,000 K) becoming the future best practice reference for iPV performance evaluation and recommend its adoption in the forthcoming IEC technical specifications.
insights.locator: Recommendation for a future best practice WLED reference

insights.claim: Because fluorescent lamps are being phased out under legislation in the EU, USA, China and 147 countries since 2023, phosphor-converted white LEDs or hybrid RGBW WLEDs are recommended as the natural reference technology for indoor PV testing.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The regulatory death of fluorescent lighting removes it as a valid reference and forces the field onto LED spectra.
insights.quote: Since 2023, the European Union, the USA, China and 147 countries have enacted agreements or legislation to phase out fluorescent lamps

insights.claim: Detailed balance limit calculations show maximum theoretical indoor PV efficiency under the five CIE LED illuminants ranges from 55.9% to 57.8%, with maximum power densities of 35.0 to 37.1 microwatts per square centimeter at 200 lx.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Sets the physical ceiling against which reported iPV efficiencies and current densities can be sanity-checked for plausibility.

insights.claim: Amorphous silicon remains the dominant commercial indoor PV technology at 7-16% efficiency, while next-generation organic, perovskite, dye-sensitized and III-V devices have reached 30-45% at small laboratory-cell level indoors.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The efficiency gap between incumbent a-Si modules and emerging lab cells signals where commercial disruption and academic investment are concentrated.

insights.claim: The consensus identifies 200 lx as the primary illuminance at which indoor PV performance must always be reported, noting it is the only level at which all 15 surveyed commercial indoor-PV manufacturers publish device performance.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A mandatory single reporting illuminance lets buyers and investors compare vendor datasheets on a like-for-like basis.
insights.quote: 200 lx is the only illuminance level at which all 15 companies provide performance of their PV devices

insights.claim: Wall-mounted positions typical for IoT devices measured only 60-200 lx and ceiling positions just 30-50 lx in a real office, well below the 200-500 lx recommended for desk surfaces, underscoring that device placement strongly affects available indoor light.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: IoT designers must size iPV harvesters for the dim wall and ceiling locations where sensors actually sit, not desk-level brightness.

insights.claim: Uncalibrated general-purpose luxmeters, historically calibrated to incandescent illuminant A, produced illuminance-reading discrepancies of up to 25% versus a calibrated spectroradiometer under identical 200 lx white-LED conditions, while an NIST-traceable luxmeter stayed within 5%.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Cheap uncalibrated meters silently inflate or deflate reported iPV efficiencies, so NMI-traceable calibration is essential for defensible numbers.
insights.quote: Discrepancies of even 25% were found using non-calibrated equipment.

insights.claim: Comparative studies show efficiency measurement ambiguities of roughly 2% using power-control illuminance adjustment versus 6-15% using optical-attenuation methods, making current-driven power control the preferred intensity-adjustment approach.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Choice of intensity-control hardware alone can swing measured efficiency by up to 15%, so labs should default to power control.
insights.quote: Comparative studies have shown efficiency measurement ambiguities of approximately 2% with IAS-P and 6–15% with IAS-O methods

insights.claim: For small laboratory cells under non-collimated light, black opaque masking cut short-circuit-current overestimation in perovskite solar cells from 39% (unmasked 4x4 mm device) to 5% with a 3.5x3.5 mm mask aperture at 1,000 lx.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Unmasked small-cell measurements can overstate current by nearly 40%, a common source of inflated record-efficiency claims.

insights.claim: The authors introduce four base stability tests for indoor PV inspired by ISOS protocols, with light-soaking and measurement at 1,000 lx (labeled BPIM-L1k) designated the main best practice because degradation mechanisms are more observable at higher lux.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Standardized stability tests address a critical gap, since lifespan and degradation directly determine iPV levelized cost and commercial viability.

insights.claim: Because indoor PV operates in mild environments, the time to decay to 80% of initial efficiency may exceed practical timeframes, so the authors recommend ageing samples at least 1,000 hours and, alternatively, using elevated illuminance of 1,000-20,000 lx to accelerate degradation to a practical t80.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Sets a minimum credible stability-testing duration so vendors cannot claim durability from short or non-standard ageing runs.
